pitch:
Check - the - receipt is about Trace, the Data Foundation's registry for AI training data. Trace has more than 250 million receipts, and each one says where a file came from, which app collected it, and which terms the contributor accepted. The problem is that you are asked to trust those receipts, so I built a page where anyone can check one from the outside using only public data. The hash and signature checks run right in your browser.

I also ran an audit on October 28. A script picked 1,000 random receipts and ran all three checks on each one. Nine didn't build the route, and those were all unsigned Numo receipts, so the page says it can't check them yet. It doesn't call them changed.

pitch:
Zcash light wallets read their memos by asking the server for each received
transaction by txid. That request tells the server which payments are yours.
Blindfetch answers the same request over private information retrieval (PIR):
the wallet gets its transaction, checks it against the txid, and the server
cannot tell which one it sent. A light wallet finds its payments by trial-decrypting compact blocks
(ZIP 307). Compact blocks carry only the first
52 bytes of each note ciphertext: enough to find a note and its value, not
enough for the memo. So the wallet asks lightwalletd for the whole
transaction, by txid. In librustzcash this is
TransactionDataRequest::Enhancement, and zcash-devtool's own enhance
command carries a TODO about it ("Create an isolated lightwalletd connection
for each transaction... with timing noise"). Every one of those requests names a transaction you received. One session, one
IP, a list of your payments. 1. Index. bf-indexer walks the chain from Ironwood activation and keeps
   every transaction with a shielded output. It zeroes the proofs and
   signatures, which sit outside the txid (ZIP 244, ZIP 229), and collapses
   the zeros. All of mainnet since Ironwood, 410,977 transactions, goes from
   5.16 GB as mined to 1.09 GB, and every one still hashes to its txid.
2. Serve. bf-server packs them into 32 KiB rows and answers YPIR queries
   over the rows. YPIR comes from valar-ypir, the Zellic-audited crate ZODL
   uses for private nullifier lookups in shielded voting.
3. Fetch. A wallet already knows where its transactions were mined. It
   downloads the whole index (a few bytes per transaction), finds its rows,
   and asks for them in rounds of exactly four queries, with queries for
   random rows shuffled in. It fetches one round after every sync, whether or
   not anything arrived, so the timing of fetches says nothing either.
4. Verify. The wallet checks every row, dummies too, against a hash in the
   index and recomputes each transaction's txid. A server that sends anything
   wrong is locked out, and a scheduled wallet keeps sending it dummy ticks so
   the server cannot tell which wallet caught it. --compare-with checks the
   index against a second server before any query. On an Apple M1 laptop, against the full mainnet database (410,977
transactions): a round of four queries is 4.06 MiB up and 0.47 MiB down and
takes about 4.6 s. Through the public URL it takes longer, most of it the home
connection the server sits on. Mobile wallets fetch one round per sync. Details in docs/MEASUREMENTS.md. Read docs/THREAT-MODEL.md and
docs/WHAT-IS-REAL.md. In short: transactions mined
before Ironwood activation are not covered, the newest blocks are covered once
the server catches up, PIR does nothing for your IP address, and the public
server is one small cloud machine run by the author.

pitch: For India's RTI filers: know your deadlines today, and protect your evidence if the work turns dangerous. The Union government told the Rajya Sabha that 17,50,863 RTI applications were filed in 2023-24 (ETV Bharat). When a Public Information Officer misses the 30-day deadline, the filer has to know the date, treat the silence as a refusal, and file a First Appeal in time. Second appeals then wait: 4,13,972 appeals and complaints were pending across India's 29 information commissions on 30 June 2025, and a matter filed with the Telangana commission on 1 July 2025 has an estimated wait of 29 years and 2 months (Satark Nagrik Sangathan, report card 2024-25). Miss a window and the request is lost. The RTI clock works on a real application today. Enter the date the PIO received it, and it gives the reply deadline (section 7(1)), the date silence counts as refusal (7(2)), the First Appeal window (19(1)), the date the First Appellate Authority must decide (19(6)) and the Second Appeal window (19(3)), shows the backlog at your state's information commission, and drafts the First Appeal in English, हिन्दी or తెలుగు. A filer can also add their application, anonymously, to a public count per commission kept on Arkiv; the page reads how many recorded applications each commission is waiting on, and how many are past their reply deadline, with a range query on the node. What you type stays in your browser. If you choose to record the application, Arkiv gets only a salted commitment that reveals nothing about it or you. Used on a real application. On 20 October 2026 a person outside the team (a relative of the builder, unnamed by choice) filed a real RTI application with the Central Information Commission and recorded it with the RTI clock at 13:42 IST. The record is on Arkiv: open it on the RTI clock, entity 0xaf4321fc…7d2e75, written by a one-time key 0xBf35…3A39 in transaction 0x8610378a…c3c1 at block 817078. It holds only a salted commitment, so nothing about the application or the filer is on chain; the filer keeps the receipt that ties it to their application. The clock gives the reply deadline as 19 November 2026, and the record stays on Arkiv through both appeal windows after that. They did not add it to the public count. This is one filer, not a pilot. For the few whose RTI work puts them in danger, the vault is the next layer. CHRI counts at least 107 RTI users murdered since 2005. Seal your documents and check in with one tap. If you stop, the custodians you chose can open them, and nobody can delete the record: not you, not us, not whoever comes for you. The vault runs on Arkiv's testnet, so for now it is a working rehearsal. Built on Arkiv, the Web3 database, for Arkiv: Global Tour Stop (9 to 18 October 2026). Tracks: Best Indian Use Case, Censorship Resistance, Privacy, Security, Open Source. All documents in this build are synthetic and the network is a testnet. Testnet versus real use: this build proves the design end to end on Tiramisu. Real ac

pitch: Trace, the DATA Foundation's registry for AI training data, has recorded more than 250 million receipts. Each one says where a file came from, which app collected it, which terms the contributor accepted, and when it was registered. Each check also says what it doesn't prove. A valid signature shows the app vouched for those exact fields at that moment. It says nothing about whether the consent was informed or the rights are valid. All three public checks can be run by an outsider today, using only what Trace, the provider and the DATA Network explorer publish. On Oct 28, 2026 the audit script drew 1,000 receipts at random from Trace's history (registered between Jul 1 and Oct 26, 2026) and ran the three public checks on each. The nine receipts whose fields didn't rebuild the root are all unsigned Numo receipts from the Numo Mobile and Poseidon Season 1 clients. Their roots are on chain like every other receipt's. Those apps don't sign, so there's no way to tell from outside how they built the root. The page reports them as "can't check this yet" and doesn't treat them as changed. Numo and oto receipts (57 in the sample) carry no provider signature, so check 2 doesn't apply to them. Every receipt checked is listed in results/audit-20261028.json, with the summary in results/audit-20261028.md. To redraw the same sample: The DATA Network and Trace are moving to Sui, and Walrus becomes the default storage layer for DATA Foundation apps. Under the announced plan, Trace would keep an encrypted copy of each original on Walrus, with access controlled by Seal. A licensed buyer could then run check 4 against the stored original. The page shows this behind a "With Walrus on Sui (planned)" switch and never runs a check against it. The current DATA Network keeps running until the upgrade, and holders don't need to do anything. Sources: Sui announcement, DATA on Sui docs. The server only proxies public data, because Trace doesn't send CORS headers. Every hash and signature check runs in the browser. Responses are cached, and the featured receipt has a saved copy so the page still works if a source is slow. An independent project. Not made by or affiliated with the DATA Foundation, Sui or Walrus. MIT licensed.

pitch: Say what your project does, and Nijam checks every claim against the code. You paste a public GitHub link and pitch the project out loud, the way you would to a judge. Nijam splits the pitch into claims, reads the repo at one commit, and gives each claim a verdict with the lines behind it. Nijam means truth in Telugu. I built it because solo hackathon work ends with claims I have to check by hand before I submit. Spoken claims are the ones that reach judges, so that is what it checks. It has two modes. My pitch checks what you say about the project. What I told my tools checks the instructions you dictated to a coding tool, and tells you what to say next for anything that did not get built. public/history.mjs pulls those instructions from your local Wispr Flow history. It is read-only and sends nothing anywhere. Flow's history file is undocumented, so an update can break it. A language model reads the code and proposes a verdict. Code in src/lib/gate.ts then decides whether the proposal stands: Each report also gives you a WHAT-IS-REAL.md, an honest rewrite of the pitch, and a receipt: a SHA-256 hash over the commit, the text and the verdicts, signed with Ed25519. The browser can check both. The signature shows Nijam issued the report, and it does not make the verdicts true. Nijam reads code and does not run it. It cannot prove that something is deployed or that a number was measured. The gate confirms a quote exists, and it cannot confirm the model read it correctly or that the code is ever called, so dead code can pass. Pitches and repo excerpts go to a third-party language model, so it only accepts public repos. Set LLM_PROVIDER, LLM_API_KEY, LLM_MODEL, GITHUB_TOKEN and RECEIPT_KEY in .env.local. LLM_PROVIDER=gemini uses Gemini; any other value uses Anthropic. npm run eval scores the checker on a planted repo with hand-labelled answers in eval/labelled.ts.
